claim: Metagenomic studies of environmental samples have uncovered a great diversity of viruses that have a pervasive presence in the biosphere.
source: Metagenomic studies of environmental samples have uncovered a great diversity of viruses that have a pervasive presence in the biosphere (Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018; Greninger, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018; Greninger, 2018).

claim: Viral diversity is especially overwhelming in RNA viruses that infect animal hosts.
source: This diversity is especially overwhelming in RNA viruses that infect animal hosts (Shi et al., 2016; Dolja and Koonin, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Shi et al., 2016; Dolja and Koonin, 2018).

claim: Viruses rely on capturing cellular ribosomes to gain access to the host machinery for protein production.
source: As strict cellular parasites, viruses rely on capturing cellular ribosomes to gain access to the host machinery for protein production (Jan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Jan et al., 2016).

claim: The eukaryotic translation machinery is complex and sophisticated, involving large, multi-component protein factors that assist in the operation of eukaryotic ribosomes.
source: In eukaryotes, especially in animals, this machinery is complex and sophisticated, involving large, multi-component protein factors that assist in the operation of eukaryotic ribosomes (Hashem and Frank, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hashem and Frank, 2018).

claim: Translation in eukaryotes conserves four main phases: initiation, elongation, termination and recycling.
source: Although complex, translation in eukaryotes conserves four main phases that are also found in its prokaryotic counterparts, namely: initiation, elongation, termination and recycling (Schmeing and Ramakrishnan, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Schmeing and Ramakrishnan, 2009).

claim: Initiation is significantly expanded in eukaryotes, with two GTP-regulated steps required for the correct positioning of the first aminoacyl-tRNA.
source: Initiation is significantly expanded in eukaryotes, with two GTP-regulated steps required for the correct positioning of the first aminoacyl-tRNA responsible for setting up the correct reading frame on the messenger RNA (mRNA) (Jackson et al., 2010; Aitken and Lorsch, 2012; Myasnikov et al., 2009; Hinnebusch, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Jackson et al., 2010; Aitken and Lorsch, 2012; Myasnikov et al., 2009; Hinnebusch, 2014).

claim: Eukaryotic initiation starts when the 40S subunit together with initiation factors eIF1, eIF1A, eIF3, eIF5 and the Ternary Complex form the 43S Pre-Initiation Complex.
source: Eukaryotic initiation starts when the 40S subunit together with the initiation factors eIF1, eIF1A, eIF3, eIF5 and the Ternary Complex (TC) (eIF2–Met-tRNAiMet–GTP) form the 43S Pre-Initiation Complex (43S-PIC), which is competent for mRNA recruitment (Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Jackson et al., 2010).

claim: Eukaryotic mRNAs are docked to the 43S-PIC at their 5' ends, forming the 48S complex.
source: Eukaryotic mRNAs are then docked to the 43S-PIC at their 5' ends, forming the 48S complex (Hinnebusch, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hinnebusch, 2017).

claim: Once the AUG codon is detected, a structural transition in the 48S from an open, scanning-competent conformation to a closed, scanning-arrested conformation occurs.
source: Once the AUG codon is detected, a structural transition in the 48S from an open, scanning-competent conformation to a closed, scanning-arrested conformation occurs (Hussain et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hussain et al., 2014).

claim: The conformational change upon AUG detection is accompanied by the release of eIF1, eIF2 and GDP, leaving the Met-tRNAiMet at the P-site of the 40S base paired with the AUG codon.
source: This conformational change is accompanied by the release of eIF1, eIF2 and GDP, leaving the Met-tRNAiMet at the P-site of the 40S base paired with the AUG codon (Aitken and Lorsch, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Aitken and Lorsch, 2012).

claim: A second GTP-regulated step, catalyzed by initiation factor eIF5B, is required for the recruitment of the large (60S) ribosomal subunit.
source: A second GTP-regulated step, catalyzed by initiation factor eIF5B, is then required for the recruitment of the large (60S) ribosomal subunit (Pestova et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Pestova et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2002).

claim: A full (80S) ribosome primed with mRNA and Met-tRNAiMet at the P-site transitions to the elongation phase.
source: A full (80S) ribosome primed with mRNA and Met-tRNAiMet at the P-site then transitions to the elongation phase (Wang et al., 2019; Voorhees and Ramakrishnan, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Wang et al., 2019; Voorhees and Ramakrishnan, 2013).

claim: The canonical translation initiation pathway is 5'-end and cap-dependent.
source: The pathway described above is called the canonical, 5'-end and cap-dependent translation route of initiation (Hinnebusch, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hinnebusch, 2014).

claim: The bulk of eukaryotic mRNAs follow the canonical translation route.
source: The bulk of eukaryotic mRNAs transitions follow this route, but deviations from the canonical route are common, and normally associated with translation under stress conditions (Starck et al., 2016; Shatsky et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Starck et al., 2016; Shatsky et al., 2010).

claim: Deviations from the canonical translation route are common and normally associated with translation under stress conditions.
source: The bulk of eukaryotic mRNAs transitions follow this route, but deviations from the canonical route are common, and normally associated with translation under stress conditions (Starck et al., 2016; Shatsky et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Starck et al., 2016; Shatsky et al., 2010).

claim: Non-canonical initiation is associated with extended 5' UnTranslated Regions (5'-UTRs) on mRNAs.
source: Non-canonical initiation is also associated with extended 5' UnTranslated Regions (5'-UTRs) on mRNAs (Sendoel et al., 2017; Young and Wek, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Sendoel et al., 2017; Young and Wek, 2016).

claim: In complex eukaryotes, 5'-UTRs can be very long and can harbor short Open Reading Frames designated as upstream ORFs (uORFs).
source: In complex eukaryotes, 5'-UTRs can be very long and can harbor short Open Reading Frames (ORFs) designated as upstream ORFs (uORFs) (Young and Wek, 2016; Wethmar, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Young and Wek, 2016; Wethmar, 2014).

claim: Well-studied examples of the functional relevance of uORFs at 5'-UTRs can be found in the yeast stress response regulator GCN4 or the mammalian transcription factor ATF4.
source: Well-studied examples of the functional relevance of uORFs at 5'-UTRs can be found in the yeast stress response regulator GCN4 or the mammalian transcription factor ATF4 (Hinnebusch, 1993; Vattem and Wek, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Hinnebusch, 1993; Vattem and Wek, 2004).

claim: uAUG codons that are immediately followed by a stop codon (designated as 'start-stop uORFs') are found in the 5'-UTRs of mammalian mRNAs.
source: uAUG codons that are immediately followed by a stop codon (designated as 'start-stop uORFs') are also found in the 5'-UTRs of mammalian mRNAs (Wethmar, 2014; Gunišová et al., 2018), but little is known about how these 'start-stop uORFs' regulate translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Wethmar, 2014; Gunišová et al., 2018).

claim: Little is known about how 'start-stop uORFs' regulate translation.
source: uAUG codons that are immediately followed by a stop codon (designated as 'start-stop uORFs') are also found in the 5'-UTRs of mammalian mRNAs (Wethmar, 2014; Gunišová et al., 2018), but little is known about how these 'start-stop uORFs' regulate translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statement itself, which acknowledges a gap in knowledge.

claim: Viruses exploit the complexity of eukaryotic initiation to gain access to the host machinery for protein production.
source: Viruses exploit the complexity of eukaryotic initiation to gain access to the host machinery for protein production (Jaafar and Kieft, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Jaafar and Kieft, 2019).

claim: Strategies such as mimicking the cap structure or transferring caps from cellular mRNAs ('cap-snatching') allow viral mRNAs to hijack host ribosomes.
source: Strategies such as mimicking the cap structure or transferring caps from cellular mRNAs ('cap-snatching') allow viral mRNAs to hijack host ribosomes, redirecting them towards the production of viral proteins (Jan et al., 2016; Jaafar and Kieft, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Jan et al., 2016; Jaafar and Kieft, 2019).

claim: A prominent viral strategy for ribosome hijacking is the use of structured RNA sequences in viral mRNAs called Internal Ribosomal Entry Sites (IRES).
source: A more prominent viral strategy for ribosome hijacking is the use of structured RNA sequences in viral mRNAs (Yamamoto et al., 2017). These sequences are called Internal Ribosomal Entry Sites (IRES), and a tentative classification based on their degree of RNA structure and dependency on canonical initiation factors divided them in four main types (Filbin and Kieft, 2009; Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Yamamoto et al., 2017; Filbin and Kieft, 2009; Johnson et al., 2017).

claim: A tentative classification of IRESs based on their degree of RNA structure and dependency on canonical initiation factors divided them in four main types.
source: These sequences are called Internal Ribosomal Entry Sites (IRES), and a tentative classification based on their degree of RNA structure and dependency on canonical initiation factors divided them in four main types (Filbin and Kieft, 2009; Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Filbin and Kieft, 2009; Johnson et al., 2017).

claim: The Dicistroviridae family of positive single-stranded RNA viruses employs two types of IRESs to express the regulatory versus the structural genes differentially.
source: The Dicistroviridae family of positive single-stranded RNA ((+)-ssRNA) viruses employs two types of IRESs to express the regulatory versus the structural genes differentially (Nakashima and Uchiumi, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Nakashima and Uchiumi, 2009).

claim: The genome architecture of Dicistroviruses functionally segregates both kinds of genes in two ORFs.
source: The genome architecture of these viruses functionally segregates both kinds of genes in two ORFs (Figure 1A; Hertz and Thompson, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hertz and Thompson, 2011) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The first ORF of Dicistroviruses is preceded by an approximately 700-nucleotide 5'-UTR, which harbors an IRES assigned to the type III family.
source: The first ORF is preceded by an approximately 700-nucleotide 5'-UTR, which harbors an IRES assigned to the type III family (Gross et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Gross et al., 2017).

claim: In vitro characterization of the 5'-UTR-IRES of the Cricket Paralysis Virus narrowed down the region of the 5'-UTR responsible for the IRES activity and established the strict requirement of eIF3 for this IRES to initiate translation.
source: In vitro characterization of the 5'-UTR-IRES of the Cricket Paralysis Virus (CrPV), a prototypical Dicistrovirus, narrowed down the region of the 5'-UTR responsible for the IRES activity and established the strict requirement of eIF3 for this IRES to initiate translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of in vitro characterization experiments.

claim: The AUG codon of the CrPV ORF1 is immediately preceded by a 'start-stop uORF'.
source: Interestingly, the AUG codon of the CrPV ORF1 is immediately preceded by a 'start-stop uORF' (Gross et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Gross et al., 2017).

claim: The 5'-UTR-IRES does not form a stable complex with the 40S in the absence of eIF3.
source: Unexpectedly, the 5'-UTR-IRES does not form a stable complex with the 40S in the absence of eIF3, in contrast to the HCV-IRES, which is able to form stable complexes with the 40S subunit alone and even with full (80S) ribosomes (Figure 1B; Yokoyama et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and a citation to a published study (Yokoyama et al., 2019).

claim: The HCV-IRES is able to form stable complexes with the 40S subunit alone and even with full (80S) ribosomes.
source: Unexpectedly, the 5'-UTR-IRES does not form a stable complex with the 40S in the absence of eIF3, in contrast to the HCV-IRES, which is able to form stable complexes with the 40S subunit alone and even with full (80S) ribosomes (Figure 1B; Yokoyama et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and a citation to a published study (Yokoyama et al., 2019).

claim: In the presence of eIF3, the 5'-UTR-IRES co-migrates with purified 40S subunits.
source: In the presence of eIF3, however, the 5'-UTR-IRES co-migrates with purified 40S subunits (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The 40S–5'-UTR-IRES–eIF3 complex revealed clear particles in cryo-EM images, rendering detailed two-dimensional class averages in which density for eIF3 could be identified.
source: This complex revealed clear particles in cryo-EM images, rendering detailed two-dimensional class averages in which density for eIF3 could be identified, albeit at lower threshold (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 40S–5'-UTR-IRES–eIF3 complex exhibited a delicate behavior under cryo-EM conditions, with a strong tendency to disassemble in thin ice.
source: The 40S–5'-UTR-IRES–eIF3 complex exhibited a delicate behavior under cryo-EM conditions, with a strong tendency to disassemble in thin ice.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection.

claim: Extensive screening for suitable ice areas was essential to obtain particles of the fully assembled complex.
source: Extensive screening for suitable ice areas was essential to obtain particles of the fully assembled complex (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on observations during cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection, with reference to Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sample exhibited a high degree of heterogeneity, which could be resolved by image processing in Relion.
source: The sample also exhibited a high degree of heterogeneity, which could be resolved by image processing in Relion (Scheres, 2012; Scheres, 2016; Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by image processing data shown in Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and citations to Relion software publications (Scheres, 2012; Scheres, 2016).

claim: Two main classes of particles containing density for 5'-UTR-IRES, 40S and eIF3 were found in the dataset.
source: Two main classes of particles containing density for 5'-UTR-IRES, 40S and eIF3 were found in the dataset (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Both classes contain density for the 40S, the IRES and the core subunits of eIF3 (a/c/e/k/l/f/m).
source: Both classes contain density for the 40S, the IRES and the core subunits of eIF3 (a/c/e/k/l/f/m), and class-2 also presents density for eIF3 subunit d (Figure 1E, eIF3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Class-2 presents density for eIF3 subunit d.
source: Both classes contain density for the 40S, the IRES and the core subunits of eIF3 (a/c/e/k/l/f/m), and class-2 also presents density for eIF3 subunit d (Figure 1E, eIF3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Class-2 exhibits a 40S head in a swiveled configuration.
source: Class-2 exhibits a 40S head in a swiveled configuration.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: In the swiveled configuration of the 40S head, eIF3d establishes interactions with eIF3a, a core subunit of eIF3.
source: Owing to this swiveled configuration of the 40S head, eIF3d establishes interactions with eIF3a, a core subunit of eIF3 (see below).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: The ribosome-bound conformation of 5'-UTR-IRES shows an extended configuration, almost circling the 40S head.
source: The ribosome-bound conformation of 5'-UTR-IRES shows an extended configuration, almost circling the 40S head (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three domains connected by flexible linkers could be defined in the 5'-UTR-IRES: an elongated domain I (DI) at the back of the 40S head contacting ribosomal proteins uS3 and RACK1, a second domain (DII) formed by a dual hairpin at the back of the 40S body interacting with eIF3, and a third, large helical domain (DIII) placed at the periphery of the 40S E-site, contacting ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11.
source: Three domains connected by flexible linkers could be defined: an elongated domain I (DI) at the back of the 40S head contacting ribosomal proteins uS3 and RACK1 (Figure 2), a second domain (DII) formed by a dual hairpin at the back of the 40S body interacting with eIF3 (Figure 3), and a third, large helical domain (DIII) placed at the periphery of the 40S E-site, contacting ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11 (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: The 5' proximal segment of the 5'-UTR-IRES (residues 357 to 486) forms domain I, which is characterized by an elongated T-shaped structure anchored to the back of the 40S head.
source: The 5' proximal segment of the 5'-UTR-IRES (residues 357 to 486) forms domain I, which is characterized by an elongated T-shaped structure anchored to the back of the 40S head (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: A long helical segment in domain I 'wraps' around the apical part of ribosomal protein RACK1.
source: A long helical segment in this domain 'wraps' around the apical part of ribosomal protein RACK1.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: Two bases of the helical segment of domain I, C442 and C444, are extruded from the body of the double helix to establish hydrophobic interactions with tyrosine residue 140 of RACK1.
source: Two bases of this helical segment of domain I, C442 and C444, are extruded from the body of the double helix to establish hydrophobic interactions with tyrosine residue 140 of RACK1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: These interactions bend the main helical segment of the 5'-UTR-IRES DI, directing the tip of this domain towards ribosomal protein uS3.
source: These interactions bend the main helical segment of the 5'-UTR-IRES DI, directing the tip of this domain towards ribosomal protein uS3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Guanine residue 395 is inserted deep into a hydrophobic pocket of ribosomal protein uS3, establishing contacts with main-chain atoms of this ribosomal protein.
source: Guanine residue 395 is inserted deep into a hydrophobic pocket of ribosomal protein uS3, establishing contacts with main-chain atoms of this ribosomal protein.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: In this location, 5'-UTR-IRES DI is found adjacent to the mRNA entry channel of the 40S, overlapping with the space previously described as being occupied by the helicase DHX29 involved in canonical initiation.
source: In this location, 5'-UTR-IRES DI is found adjacent to the mRNA entry channel of the 40S, overlapping with the space previously described as being occupied by the helicase DHX29 involved in canonical initiation (Figure 2D; Hashem et al., 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2D and a citation to a published study (Hashem et al., 2013a).

claim: The second domain of 5'-UTR-IRES (DII) is connected to domain I by a flexible linker that is poorly defined in the maps as it is exposed to the solvent.
source: The second domain of 5'-UTR-IRES (DII) is connected to domain I by a flexible linker that is poorly defined in our maps as it is exposed to the solvent.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: The second domain of the 5'-UTR-IRES is formed by a dual hairpin and is wedged between the back of the body of the 40S and eIF3 subunits a and c.
source: This second domain of the 5'-UTR-IRES is formed by a dual hairpin and is wedged between the back of the body of the 40S and eIF3 subunits a and c (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Ribosomal protein uS17 peripherally contacts domain II, establishing interactions with the phosphate backbone of the IRES.
source: Ribosomal protein uS17 peripherally contacts this domain, establishing interactions with the phosphate backbone of the IRES (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A network of interactions involving eIF3 subunits a, c and h anchors DII to its position.
source: A network of interactions involving eIF3 subunits a, c and h anchors DII to this position (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The interactions between eIF3 and DII are established through contacts between positively charged residues on eIF3 and the phosphate backbone of the IRES.
source: These interactions are also established through contacts between positively charged residues on eIF3 and the phosphate backbone of the IRES.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: No contacts with specific IRES bases could be observed in the eIF3-DII interaction.
source: No contacts with specific IRES bases could be observed.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: The positioning of eIF3 relative to the 40S in the 40S–5'-UTR-IRES–eIF3 complex is very similar to the canonical 48S complex and different from the position adopted by eIF3 in the CSFV-IRES–40S complex.
source: Comparisons of these structures with our complex reveal a positioning of eIF3 relative to the 40S that is very similar to the canonical 48S complex and different from the position adopted by eIF3 in the CSFV-IRES–40S complex (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparisons shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the 48S canonical configuration, eIF3 contacts the 40S through helix 1 of eIF3a and helix 22 of eIF3c, as well as through eIF3d, which is isolated in its 40S interaction, away from the core subunits of eIF3.
source: In the 48S canonical configuration, eIF3 contacts the 40S through helix 1 of eIF3a and helix 22 of eIF3c, as well as through eIF3d, which is isolated in its 40S interaction, away from the core subunits of eIF3 (Figure 3D, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3D, left.

claim: The CSFV-IRES engages the 40S, displacing eIF3 from its position in the canonical 48S.
source: The CSFV-IRES engages the 40S, displacing eIF3 from its position in the canonical 48S (Figure 3D, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3D, right.

claim: In the canonical 48S complex, eIF3 interacts with the 40S peripherally, allowing the formation of cavities between eIF3 and the back of the 40S.
source: In addition, in the canonical 48S complex, eIF3 interacts with the 40S peripherally, allowing the formation of cavities between eIF3 and the back of the 40S.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: These cavities are exploited by the 5'-UTR-IRES, which inserts its domain II into one of them, adopting a configuration that is compatible with the binding of eIF3 to the 40S in the canonical 48S complex.
source: These cavities are exploited by the 5'-UTR-IRES, which inserts its domain II into one of them, adopting a configuration that is compatible with the binding of eIF3 to the 40S in the canonical 48S complex (Figure 3D, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3D, middle.

claim: No major rearrangement of eIF3 (compared to its position in the canonical 48S complex) is required for the binding of the 5'-UTR-IRES.
source: No major rearrangement of eIF3 (compared to its position in the canonical 48S complex) is required for the binding of the 5'-UTR-IRES, so there could be an advantage in hijacking preformed cellular 48S complexes that are ready to transit the cap-dependent route of initiation.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: There could be an advantage in hijacking preformed cellular 48S complexes that are ready to transit the cap-dependent route of initiation.
source: No major rearrangement of eIF3 (compared to its position in the canonical 48S complex) is required for the binding of the 5'-UTR-IRES, so there could be an advantage in hijacking preformed cellular 48S complexes that are ready to transit the cap-dependent route of initiation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from structural data.

claim: A flexible single stranded linker connects DII with DIII, threading through the 40S channel formed by ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11.
source: Threading through the 40S channel formed by ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11, a flexible single stranded linker connects DII with DIII (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DIII forms a prominent, helical mass in the surroundings of the E-site of the small subunit at the inter-subunit face of the 40S.
source: DIII forms a prominent, helical mass in the surroundings of the E-site of the small subunit at the inter-subunit face of the 40S.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: The helical segment of DIII is very well defined in the maps because it is stabilized by numerous contacts with ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11 and with 18S ribosomal RNA bases.
source: The helical segment is very well defined in our maps because it is stabilized by numerous contacts with ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11 and with 18S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) bases (Figure 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distal part of DIII forms two short stem loops that, given their flexibility, could only be modelled at low resolution.
source: However, the distal part of this domain forms two short stem loops that, given their flexibility, could only be modelled at low resolution.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: Inspection of the cryo-EM density revealed a distortion in the canonical double helix of the main segment of DIII as it approaches the E-site.
source: Inspection of the cryo-EM density reveled a distortion in the canonical double helix of the main segment of this domain as it approaches the E-site.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: The quality of the maps in the DIII area allowed de novo modelling of these residues, revealing a set of non-canonical interactions between the RNA bases.
source: The quality of the maps in this area allowed de novo modelling of these residues, revealing a set of non-canonical interactions between the RNA bases (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: In-plane triple-base interactions involving sugar and the Hoogsteen edges of the bases, as well as purine–purine Hoogsteen base pairs, could be found in the helical segment of DIII.
source: In-plane triple-base interactions involving sugar and the Hoogsteen edges of the bases, as well as purine–purine Hoogsteen base pairs, could be found in this stretch of residues of the helical segment of DIII (Figure 4B; Leontis and Westhof, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4B and a citation to a published study (Leontis and Westhof, 1998).

claim: These non-canonical base pairs induce a distortion at the base of DIII that helps to position the single-stranded segment of the 5'-UTR-IRES harboring the uAUG codon at position 701 in the mRNA-binding channel of the 40S.
source: Overall, these non-canonical base pairs induce a distortion at the base of DIII that helps to position the single-stranded segment of the 5'-UTR-IRES harboring the uAUG codon at position 701 in the mRNA-binding channel of the 40S (Figure 4C, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4C, middle.

claim: The 5'-UTR-IRES accesses the 40 S P-site through the E-site, blocking a concurrent recruitment of the TC (eIF2–Met-tRNAiMet–GTP).
source: The 5'-UTR-IRES accesses the 40 S P-site through the E-site, blocking a concurrent recruitment of the TC (eIF2–Met-tRNAiMet–GTP, Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A similar strategy of accessing the P-site through the E-site is followed by the HCV-IRES.
source: Interestingly, a similar strategy is followed by the HCV-IRES.
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison.

claim: A superposition of the structure of the HCV-IRES in complex with the 40S with the 40S–5'-UTR-IRES–eIF3 structure reveals a very similar positioning of the domain II of HCV-IRES, accessing the P-site through the E-site to position the AUG codon in the surroundings of the P-site.
source: A superposition of the structure of the HCV-IRES in complex with the 40S (Yamamoto et al., 2015; Quade et al., 2015) (PDB ID 5A2Q) with our structure reveals a very similar positioning of the domain II of HCV-IRES, accessing the P-site through the E-site to position the AUG codon in the surroundings of the P-site (Figure 4C, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4C, bottom, and citations to published studies (Yamamoto et al., 2015; Quade et al., 2015).

claim: Even though both IRESs differ markedly in their interaction with the back of the 40S and eIF3, both converge to similar structural solutions for the placement of the AUG initial codon close to the 40 S P-site.
source: Even though both IRESs differ markedly in their interaction with the back of the 40S and eIF3, both converge to similar structural solutions for the placement of the AUG initial codon close to the 40 S P-site.
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison.

claim: Initial processing of the cryo-EM data revealed flexibility of the 40S head.
source: Initial processing of the cryo-EM data revealed flexibility of the 40S head.
evidence: The claim is based on cryo-EM data processing.

claim: Masked classification and refinement in Relion3 revealed two major populations of particles, which differ in the degrees of 40S head swiveling.
source: Masked classification and refinement in Relion3 (Zivanov et al., 2018) revealed two major populations of particles, which differ in the degrees of 40S head swiveling (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data processing shown in Figure 1 and a citation to Relion3 software (Zivanov et al., 2018).

claim: The 40S head is attached to the body by a single RNA helix, making this component of the ribosome extremely flexible.
source: The 40S head is attached to the body by a single RNA helix, making this component of the ribosome extremely flexible (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Johnson et al., 2017).

claim: Intrinsic and independent movements of the 40S head are instrumental in tRNA translocation and also in canonical initiation.
source: Intrinsic and independent movements of the 40S head are instrumental in tRNA translocation and also in canonical initiation (Ratje et al., 2010; Flis et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Ratje et al., 2010; Flis et al., 2018).

claim: The 5'-UTR-IRES exploits the intrinsic dynamic of the 40S head to bind to the 40S and then to 'lock' the IRES in a specific conformation that commits the complex towards viral translation.
source: The 5'-UTR-IRES seems to exploit this intrinsic dynamic to bind to the 40S and then to 'lock' the IRES in a specific conformation that commits the complex towards viral translation (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In class-1 (open conformation), the head of the 40S shows an almost canonical configuration with very little swiveling and no tilt.
source: In class-1 (open conformation), the head of the 40S shows an almost canonical configuration with very little swiveling and no tilt.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: In class-1, the latch of the 40S is closed.
source: In this conformation, the latch of the 40S (an early defined contact between the head and the body of the 40S [Frank et al., 1995]) is closed.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data and a citation to a published study (Frank et al., 1995).

claim: In class-1, access to the channel formed by ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11 is exposed and eIF3d density is not well defined, probably because of a high degree of flexibility or low occupancy.
source: At the other side of the 40S head, access to the channel formed by ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11 is exposed and eIF3d density is not well defined, probably because of a high degree of flexibility or low occupancy (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data shown in Figure 5A, left.

claim: In class-2 (closed conformation), the head of the 40S exhibits a medium-range degree of swiveling when compared to the widest displacement reported.
source: In class-2 (closed conformation), the head of the 40S exhibits a medium-range degree of swiveling when compared to the widest displacement reported (Ratje et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data and a citation to a published study (Ratje et al., 2010).

claim: In the open and closed classes, the positions of the 5'-UTR-IRES relative to the 40S head are very similar.
source: In the open and closed classes, the positions of the 5'-UTR-IRES relative to the 40S head are very similar (Figure 5A, right and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5A, right and B.

claim: In the swiveled conformation, the latch is open, and the channel formed by ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11 is plugged by eIF3d, which in this class presents robust density.
source: In the swiveled conformation, the latch is open, and the channel formed by ribosomal proteins uS7 and uS11 is plugged by eIF3d, which in this class presents robust density (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The main subunits of eIF3 (a/c/e/k/l/f/m) show a similar conformation in both classes, having a similar orientation with respect to the 40S body.
source: The main subunits of eIF3 (a/c/e/k/l/f/m) show a similar conformation in both classes, having a similar orientation with respect to the 40S body (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the swiveled configuration (class-2), the 40S head brings eIF3d close to eIF3a, one of the core subunits of eIF3.
source: In the swiveled configuration (class-2), the 40S head brings eIF3d close to eIF3a, one of the core subunits of eIF3 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Well-defined density in the eIF3a–eIF3d interface area could be observed in class-2.
source: Well-defined density in this area could be observed for the eIF3a–eIF3d interface (Figure 5C, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5C, right.

claim: This compact state of eIF3 represents a hitherto unknown conformation.
source: This compact state of eIF3 represent a hitherto unknown conformation (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Lee et al., 2016).

claim: The structures of the 40S–5'-UTR-IRES–eIF3 complex revealed a positioning of the DIII of the IRES that overlaps with the position that the TC populates at the E-site in canonical initiation.
source: Our structures of the 40S–5'-UTR-IRES–eIF3 complex revealed a positioning of the DIII of the IRES that overlaps with the position that the TC populates at the E-site in canonical initiation (Figure 4C; Hussain et al., 2014; Eliseev et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4C and citations to two published studies (Hussain et al., 2014; Eliseev et al., 2018).

claim: In the maps, density for the single-stranded segment of RNA of the IRES placed close to the P-site could only be confidently identified until residue 695, whereas the canonical AUG of ORF1 is found at nucleotide 709.
source: In addition, in our maps, we could only confidently identify density for the single-stranded segment of RNA of the IRES placed close to the P-site until residue 695, whereas the canonical AUG of ORF1 is found at nucleotide 709.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: Translation initiation factors in mammals and insects are highly homologous.
source: Translation initiation factors in mammals and insects are highly homologous.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: eIF2-alpha shares 57% identity and 74% similarity between human and Drosophila.
source: In particular, eIF2-alpha shares 57% identity and 74% similarity between human and Drosophila, eIF2-beta 74% identity and 83% similarity, eIF2-gamma 82% identity and 88% similarity, eIF5B 71% identity and 85% similarity, eIF3a 46% identity and 63% similarity, and eIF3c 51% identity and 66% similarity.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: eIF2-beta shares 74% identity and 83% similarity between human and Drosophila.
source: In particular, eIF2-alpha shares 57% identity and 74% similarity between human and Drosophila, eIF2-beta 74% identity and 83% similarity, eIF2-gamma 82% identity and 88% similarity, eIF5B 71% identity and 85% similarity, eIF3a 46% identity and 63% similarity, and eIF3c 51% identity and 66% similarity.

source: In particular, eIF2-alpha shares 57% identity and 74% similarity between human and Drosophila, eIF2-beta 74% identity and 83% similarity, eIF2-gamma 82% identity and 88% similarity, eIF5B 71% identity and 85% similarity, eIF3a 46% identity and 63% similarity, and eIF3c 51% identity and 66% similarity.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: eIF5B shares 71% identity and 85% similarity between human and Drosophila.
source: In particular, eIF2-alpha shares 57% identity and 74% similarity between human and Drosophila, eIF2-beta 74% identity and 83% similarity, eIF2-gamma 82% identity and 88% similarity, eIF5B 71% identity and 85% similarity, eIF3a 46% identity and 63% similarity, and eIF3c 51% identity and 66% similarity.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: eIF3a shares 46% identity and 63% similarity between human and Drosophila.
source: In particular, eIF2-alpha shares 57% identity and 74% similarity between human and Drosophila, eIF2-beta 74% identity and 83% similarity, eIF2-gamma 82% identity and 88% similarity, eIF5B 71% identity and 85% similarity, eIF3a 46% identity and 63% similarity, and eIF3c 51% identity and 66% similarity.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: eIF3c shares 51% identity and 66% similarity between human and Drosophila.
source: In particular, eIF2-alpha shares 57% identity and 74% similarity between human and Drosophila, eIF2-beta 74% identity and 83% similarity, eIF2-gamma 82% identity and 88% similarity, eIF5B 71% identity and 85% similarity, eIF3a 46% identity and 63% similarity, and eIF3c 51% identity and 66% similarity.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: The high level of homology between mammalian and insect initiation factors justifies the utilization of mammalian initiation factors for CrPV analysis.
source: This high level of homology justifies the utilization of mammalian initiation factors for CrPV analysis, as has been done before for the CrPV IGR-IRES.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from sequence homology data.

claim: eIF2 delivers Met-tRNAiMet to the uAUG at position 701.
source: In isolation, the TC (eIF2–Met-tRNAiMet–GTP) is able to load Met-tRNAiMet onto the P-site of the 40S–5'-UTR-IRES–eIF3 complex, producing a robust toe-print (Figure 6A, lane 2, label 48S–uAUG) 15–17 nucleotides away from the uAUG located at 701.
evidence: The claim is supported by toe-print assay data shown in Figure 6A, lane 2.

claim: A similar uAUG delivery of Met-tRNAiMet can be accomplished by eIF5B.
source: A similar uAUG delivery of Met-tRNAiMet can be accomplished by eIF5B which, under stress conditions, has been described as substituting for eIF2 in Met-tRNAiMet delivery (Terenin et al., 2008; Pestova et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2014; Kenner et al., 2019), with eukaryotic initiation then following a 'bacterial-like' mode (Figure 6A, lane 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by toe-print assay data shown in Figure 6A, lane 4, and citations to four published studies (Terenin et al., 2008; Pestova et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2014; Kenner et al., 2019).

claim: Under stress conditions, eIF5B has been described as substituting for eIF2 in Met-tRNAiMet delivery, with eukaryotic initiation then following a 'bacterial-like' mode.
source: A similar uAUG delivery of Met-tRNAiMet can be accomplished by eIF5B which, under stress conditions, has been described as substituting for eIF2 in Met-tRNAiMet delivery (Terenin et al., 2008; Pestova et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2014; Kenner et al., 2019), with eukaryotic initiation then following a 'bacterial-like' mode (Figure 6A, lane 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Terenin et al., 2008; Pestova et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2014; Kenner et al., 2019).

claim: Transitioning to the correct AUG could only be detected in the presence of eIF1 and eIF1A, and only when the TC was present, and not for eIF5B.
source: Transitioning to the correct AUG could only be detected in the presence of eIF1and eIF1A, and only when the TC was present, and not for eIF5B (Figure 6A, lanes 3 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by toe-print assay data shown in Figure 6A, lanes 3 and 5.

claim: The presence of eIF1 and eIF1A seems to be detrimental to uAUG Met-tRNAiMet loading by eIF5B, as their presence significantly reduces the toe-print signal that can be observed for eIF5B in isolation.
source: Notably, the presence of eIF1and eIF1A seems to be detrimental to uAUG Met-tRNAiMet loading by eIF5B, as their presence significantly reduces the toe-print signal that can be observed for eIF5B in isolation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from toe-print assay data.

claim: No concomitant increase in toe-print signal for the canonical AUG could be observed for the eIF1/eIF1A/eIF5B reaction.
source: However, no concomitant increase in toe-print signal for the canonical AUG could be observed for the eIF1/eIF1A/eIF5B reaction.
evidence: The claim is based on toe-print assay data.

claim: Only eIF2 as part of the TC and assisted by eIF1 and eIF1A can properly locate the bona fide AUG of ORF1.
source: Only eIF2 as part of the TC and assisted by eIF1 and eIF1A can properly locate the bona fide AUG of ORF1.
evidence: The claim is based on toe-print assay data.

claim: The role of the uAUG located at nucleotide 701 is not clear.
source: The role of the uAUG located at nucleotide 701 is not clear, but the fact that eIF5B can deliver Met-tRNAiMet only to this codon points towards an important role for this uAUG in initiation when eIF2 is unavailable.
evidence: The claim acknowledges uncertainty about the role of uAUG.

claim: The fact that eIF5B can deliver Met-tRNAiMet only to the uAUG codon points towards an important role for this uAUG in initiation when eIF2 is unavailable.
source: The role of the uAUG located at nucleotide 701 is not clear, but the fact that eIF5B can deliver Met-tRNAiMet only to this codon points towards an important role for this uAUG in initiation when eIF2 is unavailable.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Ribosome-profiling datasets have revealed the presence of translating ribosomes paused on 5'-UTRs, implying a decisive role of these sequences in regulating translation, especially under stress conditions.
source: Ribosome-profiling datasets have revealed the presence of translating ribosomes paused on 5'-UTRs, implying a decisive role of these sequences in regulating translation, especially under stress conditions (Sendoel et al., 2017; Archer et al., 2016; Andreev et al., 2015; Ingolia et al., 2009; Brar and Weissman, 2015; Resch et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to six published studies (Sendoel et al., 2017; Archer et al., 2016; Andreev et al., 2015; Ingolia et al., 2009; Brar and Weissman, 2015; Resch et al., 2009).

claim: The 5'-UTR of the (+)-ssRNA of the Dicistovirus CrPV harbors an IRES that is able to direct initiation towards ORF1 in the early phase of infection.
source: The 5'-UTR of the (+)-ssRNA of the Dicistovirus CrPV harbors an IRES that is able to direct initiation towards ORF1 in the early phase of infection (Hertz and Thompson, 2011; Garrey et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Hertz and Thompson, 2011; Garrey et al., 2010).

claim: Expression of ORF1 is instrumental for virus replication because the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), and the protease responsible for the proteolytic digestion of the polyprotein containing the structural proteins, are encoded in ORF1.
source: Expression of ORF1 is instrumental for virus replication because the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), and the protease responsible for the proteolytic digestion of the polyprotein containing the structural proteins, are encoded in ORF1 (Jan et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Jan et al., 2003).

claim: The 5'-UTR-IRES features a novel multi-domain, extended architecture that encircles three quarters of the 40S head, exploiting binding sites not previously described for any IRESs.
source: The 5'-UTR-IRES features a novel multi-domain, extended architecture that encircles three quarters of the 40S head, exploiting binding sites not previously described for any IRESs (Figures 2, 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figures 2, 3 and 4.

claim: Ribosomal proteins uS3 and RACK1 are used by the IRES to anchor its DI to the back of the 40S head.
source: Ribosomal proteins uS3 and RACK1 are used by the IRES to anchor its DI to the back of the 40S head (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The structure rationalizes previous data showing a preeminent role of RACK1 in CrPV and related viruses that infect Drosophila.
source: The structure thus rationalizes previous data showing a preeminent role of RACK1 in CrPV and related viruses that infect Drosophila (Majzoub et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Majzoub et al., 2014).

claim: The interaction of DI with RACK1 is instrumental in positioning DII at the back of the 40S body, sandwiched in between ribosomal protein uS17 and eIF3.
source: The interaction of DI with RACK1 is also instrumental in positioning DII at the back of the 40S body, sandwiched in between ribosomal protein uS17 and eIF3 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In contrast with the HCV-IRES, the conformation observed for eIF3 in the complex with 5'-UTR-IRES is very similar to that observed for eIF3 in the 48S complex, with the IRES 'filling up' cavities that are present between the 40S and eIF3 in this canonical complex.
source: Interestingly and in contrast with the HCV-IRES, the conformation observed for eIF3 in the complex with 5'-UTR-IRES is very similar to that observed for eIF3 in the 48S complex, with the IRES 'filling up' cavities that are present between the 40S and eIF3 in this canonical complex (Eliseev et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison and a citation to a published study (Eliseev et al., 2018).

claim: The HCV-IRES and related IRESs, such as the CSFV-IRES, displace eIF3 from its canonical location using a very different mechanism for IRES docking to the 40S.
source: The HCV-IRES and related IRESs, such as the CSFV-IRES, displace eIF3 from its canonical location using a very different mechanism for IRES docking to the 40S (Hashem et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hashem et al., 2013b).

claim: In order to place the AUG of ORF1 in the surroundings of the P-site, the 5'-UTR-IRES accesses the P-site through the E-site, in a manner similar to that of the HCV-IRES.
source: In order to place the AUG of ORF1 in the surroundings of the P-site, the 5'-UTR-IRES accesses the P-site through the E-site, in a manner similar to that of the HCV-IRES (Figure 4C; Yamamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4C and a citation to a published study (Yamamoto et al., 2015).

claim: The 5'-UTR-IRES recapitulates binding strategies that are known for other IRESs, such as the IGR-CrPV-IRES that also makes use of ribosomal protein uS7 for its binding to the ribosome or the HCV-IRES that places its domains II and IV in the surroundings of the P-site, sliding the elongated DII from the back of the 40S to the P-site through the E-site.
source: In this aspect, the 5'-UTR-IRES recapitulates binding strategies that are known for other IRESs, such as the IGR-CrPV-IRES that also makes use of ribosomal protein uS7 for its binding to the ribosome or the HCV-IRES that places its domains II and IV in the surroundings of the P-site, sliding the elongated DII from the back of the 40S to the P-site through the E-site (Pisareva et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Pisareva et al., 2018).

claim: The placement of the AUG of ORF1 in the surroundings of the P-site seems to be exerted by a mechanism involving the intrinsic dynamics of the 40S head.
source: The placement of the AUG of ORF1 in the surroundings of the P-site seems to be exerted by a mechanism involving the intrinsic dynamics of the 40S head (Johnson et al., 2017; Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5 and a citation to a published study (Johnson et al., 2017).

claim: The 5'-UTR-IRES exploits the characteristic swiveling movement of the 40S head to bind and progress towards a conformation that 'locks' the IRES onto the 40S, and at the same time, induces a compact conformation of eIF3 that has subunit eIF3d in close contact with the core subunits of eIF3.
source: The 5'-UTR-IRES exploits the characteristic swiveling movement of the 40S head to bind and progress towards a conformation that 'locks' the IRES onto the 40S, and at the same time, induces a compact conformation of eIF3 that has subunit eIF3d in close contact with the core subunits of eIF3 (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data and a citation to a published study (Lee et al., 2016).

claim: These dynamics are probably instrumental for the ability of the 5'-UTR-IRES–40S complex to localize the annotated AUG, in a genomic context where a uAUG-stop is physically close.
source: These dynamics are probably instrumental for the ability of the 5'-UTR-IRES–40S complex to localize the annotated AUG, in a genomic context where a uAUG-stop is physically close.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from structural data.

claim: The capacity of the 40S to scan an mRNA bidirectionally upon termination on a stop codon has been previously reported.
source: The capacity of the 40S to scan an mRNA bidirectionally upon termination on a stop codon has been previously reported (Skabkin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Skabkin et al., 2013).

claim: It is plausible that the peculiar genetic configuration of the CrPV around the annotated AUG of ORF1 evolved to leverage re-initiation mechanisms already present in the translation of cellular messengers.
source: It is thus plausible that the peculiar genetic configuration of the CrPV around the annotated AUG of ORF1 (Figure 1A) evolved to leverage these re-initiation mechanisms already present in the translation of cellular messengers.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from structural and functional data.

claim: These considerations about re-initiation mechanisms are highly speculative, as the particular role that the uAUG exerts in Met-tRNA-iMet recruitment, or more generally its involvement in initiation of viral messengers, remains enigmatic.
source: However, these considerations are highly speculative, as the particular role that the uAUG exerts in Met-tRNA-iMet recruitment, or more generally its involvement in initiation of viral messengers, remains enigmatic.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the speculative nature of the interpretation.

claim: A comprehensive understanding of the role of uAUG and the start-stop configuration will demand further studies, ideally in vivo.
source: A comprehensive understanding of the role of uAUG and the start-stop configuration will demand further studies, ideally in vivo.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the need for future research.

claim: Immediately after the (+)-ssRNA genomic molecule of the CrPV is injected into the cytoplasm of the host cell, the IRES harbored at the 5'-UTR captures 40S subunits.
source: We propose the following model for how the 5'-UTR-IRES of the CrPV operates: immediately after the (+)-ssRNA genomic molecule of the CrPV is injected into the cytoplasm of the host cell, the IRES harbored at the 5'-UTR captures 40S subunits (Figure 6B, bottom).
evidence: The claim is part of a proposed model based on structural and functional data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Recruitment of eIF3 is mediated by DII, allowing the sliding of the flexible linker connecting DII and DIII between the head and the platform of the 40S to place DIII in the surroundings of the E-site.
source: Recruitment of eIF3 is mediated by DII, allowing the sliding of the flexible linker connecting DII and DIII between the head and the platform of the 40S to place DIII in the surroundings of the E-site (Figure 6B, bottom and left).
evidence: The claim is part of a proposed model based on structural and functional data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A swivel movement of the 40S head closes the channel between the head and the platform of the 40S, effectively 'locking' the 5'-UTR-IRES into the 40S and inducing a compact conformation of eIF3 with the eIF3d subunit in interacting distance with eIF3's core subunit a.
source: A swivel movement of the 40S head closes the channel between the head and the platform of the 40S, effectively 'locking' the 5'-UTR-IRES into the 40S and inducing a compact conformation of eIF3 with the eIF3d subunit in interacting distance with eIF3's core subunit a (Figure 6B, left top).
evidence: The claim is part of a proposed model based on structural and functional data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: With this configuration, eIF2 as part of the TC can deliver Met-tRNAiMet to the uAUG located at nucleotide 701, and further assistance by initiation factors eIF1 and eIF1A allows for a downstream location of the AUG codon of ORF1 at nucleotide 709.
source: With this configuration, eIF2 as part of the TC can deliver Met-tRNAiMet to the uAUG located at nucleotide 701, and further assistance by initiation factors eIF1 and eIF1A allows for a downstream location of the AUG codon of ORF1 at nucleotide 709.
evidence: The claim is part of a proposed model based on structural and functional data.

claim: Large subunit recruitment grants transitioning towards elongation, committing the ribosome to the production of viral proteins.
source: Large subunit recruitment grants transitioning towards elongation, committing the ribosome to the production of viral proteins (Figure 6B, right top).
evidence: The claim is part of a proposed model based on structural and functional data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Given the rich diversity of viral sequences in the animal virome, new IRESs exploiting different aspects of animal translation will probably be discovered.
source: In summary, we have structurally characterized the 5'-UTR-IRES of the CrPV in its ribosome-bound state and have characterized the delivery of Met-tRNAiMet by eIF2 and eIF5B. Given the rich diversity of viral sequences in the animal virome, new IRESs exploiting different aspects of animal translation will probably be discovered.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the diversity of viral sequences.
